1.package2:
"Because of that, it seems to make it far more likely that the worse team ekes out a win. You can just play extremely conservative football, understanding that your best bet is in penalty kicks." There's no reason to believe this is true and the logic doesn't track.
Playing defensively doesn't inherently make a team worse than a team that focuses on offense.
Teams using defensive tactics can't rely on penalties to win. Most games don't have penalty tie breakers.
Penalties are used in cases of a tie, where teams are evenly matched. In terms of which team is better or worse, at that point there's no objective measurement of that. The score itself is how we measure success, and to reiterate, it's a tie. Soccer games run for 90 minutes of playtime, 120 minutes if it's a tie.
Theoretically, without a means to break the tie, a game could last forever. Penalties are the quickest way to break that tie. Penalties however have a large element of luck involved.
Penalties aren't used outside of the final brackets of tournaments because of this element. Regulation and group level matches use a points system to advance teams to the final brackets.
You would need to develop a method to break ties in the final brackets that isn't time exhaustive. Corners could be an option, but I doubt that we could keep the time they would take within a predictable pattern.

3.package1: The better team doesn't always win within the first 90 minutes of the game anyway. In that sense, a penalty shootout mirrors what makes the game of football so interesting - its unpredictability. Much of the time a team will dominate the entire match but not come out victors, falling to a defeat to a plucky underdog who managed to scrape through by creating one chance which they manage to take. That's just one example of how this system works. What penalty shoot outs do is play that unpredictability out on a grander scale. It's almost impossible to predict how they'll turn out, who will miss, who will score, which shots will be saved, and ultimately, who will win. Plus, they are an exceptionally tense examination of players' mental strengths and kicking technique, as well as goalkeeping qualities. Much of penalty taking is psychological, and it's generally the team that manages to keep their cool that comes out victor in the end. It's a brilliant, brilliant way to decide tied games and it makes for some extremely entertaining finales.

3.package3:
PK’s are a big part of them game (similar to free throws in basketball or extra points in American football). If teams were evenly matched after 120 minutes of outfield play, it is very reasonable to shift to this single component of the game in order to decide a winner. It still needs fundamental football skills plus even more mental skills (the margin for error shrinks almost to zero).

Ultimately it does not conclude that Team A is better at playing football than Team B. But it does fairly decide that Team A beat Team B while at the same time utilizing a key component of the game that takes into consideration important physical and mental characteristics
